literal: Prince of Leping Pi, in youth had talent and ability.
idiomatic: Prince of Leping, Pi, showed talent and ability from youth.

literal: In the seventh year of Taichang he was enfeoffed and appointed Grand Commandant of Cavalry.
idiomatic: In the seventh year of Taichang he received his fief and was made Grand Commandant of Cavalry.

literal: Later he supervised the armies of Hexi and Gaoping to campaign against the Southern Qin king Yang Nandang.
idiomatic: He later directed the Hexi and Gaoping armies against the Southern Qin king Yang Nandang.

literal: When the army reached Lueyang, prohibitions were uniformly strict; passing through he took nothing for himself, and the common people vied to offer cattle and wine.
idiomatic: At Lueyang his discipline was severe and impartial; the people competed to bring him cattle and wine.

literal: Nandang was afraid and returned to Chouchi.
idiomatic: Nandang, in fear, withdrew to Chouchi.

literal: And the generals deliberated, saying: "If we do not execute the powerful chiefs, after the army returns they will surely gather and become bandits."
idiomatic: The generals argued: "Unless we kill the local strongmen, they will rally into rebels once we withdraw."

literal: Also, with a great host going far out, if they take nothing by plunder there is no way to fill the army's stores and reward the officers and soldiers.
idiomatic: Besides, an army this far from home must seize something or it cannot fill its stores and pay the troops.

literal: The generals were about to follow this; at the time Secretariat Attendant Gao Yuan accompanied Pi on campaign affairs and remonstrated, saying: "If we execute them now, this injures their mind of turning to our rule; I fear that once the great army returns, rebellion will come swiftly."
idiomatic: They were about to agree when Secretariat Attendant Gao Yuan, on Pi's staff, objected: "Slaughter now will destroy their willingness to submit; the moment our main force leaves, revolt will come fast."

literal: Pi thought it correct, and thereupon soothed those newly submitting, not harming even autumn down in passing.
idiomatic: Pi accepted this and pacified the new subjects, harming not even the lightest property.

literal: Earlier, when Feng Hong fled to Goguryeo, Emperor Taiwu issued an edict to have him sent; Goguryeo did not send him.
idiomatic: Earlier, when Feng Hong had fled to Goguryeo, Emperor Taiwu ordered him handed over; Goguryeo refused.

literal: Taiwu was angry and was about to campaign against them.
idiomatic: Taiwu grew angry and prepared to attack.

literal: Pi submitted a memorial considering that with Helong newly pacified, it should be restored, making them broadly cultivate agriculture so as to enrich the army's stores, and then advance plans — they could be destroyed in one stroke.
idiomatic: Pi memorialized that Helong had only just been secured: restore it, expand farming to fill the granaries, then strike — Goguryeo could be taken at one blow.

literal: The emperor accepted it and therefore stopped.
idiomatic: The emperor agreed and dropped the campaign.

literal: Later because of the Liu Jie affair he died of grief, the matter is in the Liu Jie biography, posthumous title Prince Li.
idiomatic: He later died of grief over the Liu Jie affair, treated in Liu Jie's biography; his posthumous name was Li.

literal: Son Ba succeeded to the fief.
idiomatic: His son Ba inherited the title.

literal: Later because of an offense he was granted death, the state abolished.
idiomatic: Later, for an offense, he was ordered to die and the fief was abolished.

literal: At Pi's death and the death of the day-augur Dong Daoxiu, Gao Yuan thereupon wrote "On Divination," saying: "Formerly at the end of Emperor Mingyuan, the White Tower was raised, its height more than twenty zhang."
idiomatic: After Pi's death and the execution of the day-augur Dong Daoxiu, Gao Yuan wrote On Divination: "At the end of Emperor Mingyuan's reign a White Tower was built, more than twenty zhang high."

literal: Prince of Leping once dreamed of climbing atop it, looking in the four directions and seeing nothing.
idiomatic: The Prince of Leping once dreamed he climbed it and looked about on every side but saw nothing.

literal: The prince asked the day-augur Dong Daoxiu.
idiomatic: The prince asked Dong Daoxiu to divine it.

literal: He divined and said: "Great good fortune."
idiomatic: Daoxiu cast the hexagrams and said, "Great good fortune."

literal: The prince was silent but had a pleased expression.
idiomatic: The prince said nothing, but his face showed delight.

literal: Later when the matter broke out, the prince thereupon died in worry, while Daoxiu was executed in the marketplace.
idiomatic: When the affair broke, the prince died in grief; Daoxiu was executed in the market.

literal: If Daoxiu had pushed the six lines to answer the prince saying: "The Changes says 'the dragon exalted has regret.'"
idiomatic: Had Daoxiu read the six lines and told the prince, "The Changes says: 'The exalted dragon has regret,'"

literal: "Reaching the heights daily exalted, high yet without people — this is not good."
idiomatic: "to rise daily higher, lofty yet without support — that is not auspicious,"

literal: If it were thus, then above he would be secure for the prince, below he would preserve himself, fortune and rank would be arriving — how could there be calamity?
idiomatic: then above he would have kept the prince safe, below preserved himself, and fortune would have come — how could disaster follow?

literal: Now abandoning the root and following the tip, the arrival of blame and ill omen — is it not fitting!
idiomatic: But he forsook the root for the branch; blame and ruin came — as they should.

literal: Prince of Anding Mi, enfeoffed seventh year of Taichang.
idiomatic: Prince of Anding, Mi, was enfeoffed in the seventh year of Taichang.

literal: Died, posthumous title Prince Shang.
idiomatic: He died; his posthumous name was Shang.

literal: Without sons, state abolished.
idiomatic: He left no sons; the fief was abolished.

literal: Eldest son Liang — before Emperor Taiwu had sons, he once said: "A brother's son is like one's own son."
idiomatic: The eldest son, Liang: before Emperor Taiwu had sons of his own, he said, "A brother's son is as one's own."

literal: He personally nurtured him.
idiomatic: He raised Liang himself.

literal: When grown he was strong and brave with much knowledge, and once participated in great plans of state and army.
idiomatic: Grown, Liang was strong, brave, and well informed, and took part in major state and military decisions.

literal: In the reign of Emperor Wencheng he succeeded to the kingship, was appointed Grand General governing Chang'an and Governor of Yongzhou, and served as Inner Metropolitan Official.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Wencheng he inherited the princedom, became Grand General of Chang'an and Governor of Yongzhou, and served as Inner Metropolitan Official.

literal: Died, posthumous title Prince Jian.
idiomatic: He died; his posthumous name was Jian.

literal: Prince Jianning Chong, enfeoffed seventh year of Taichang.
idiomatic: Prince Jianning, Chong, was enfeoffed in the seventh year of Taichang.

literal: In the reign of Wencheng, Chong's son Li was enfeoffed Prince of Jinan.
idiomatic: Under Wencheng, Chong's son Li was made Prince of Jinan.

literal: Later he plotted rebellion with Prince of Jingzhao Du Yuanbao; father and son were both granted death.
idiomatic: Later he conspired with Prince of Jingzhao Du Yuanbao; father and son were both ordered to die.

literal: Prince of Xinxing Jun, enfeoffed seventh year of Taichang.
idiomatic: Prince of Xinxing, Jun, was enfeoffed in the seventh year of Taichang.

literal: In youth skilled at mounted archery, with many arts.
idiomatic: In youth he excelled at mounted archery and had many skills.

literal: Because of offense his noble title was cut to duke.
idiomatic: For an offense his rank was reduced to duke.

literal: Jun loved wine and women and often exceeded the bounds of law.
idiomatic: Jun loved wine and women and often broke the law.

literal: Also because his mother had earlier met with offense and died, while he himself had been demoted and stripped, he constantly harbored resentment and had quite a rebellious heart.
idiomatic: His mother had earlier been condemned and died; he himself had been demoted. He nursed resentment and a rebellious temper.

literal: Later when the matter broke out he was granted death, state abolished.
idiomatic: When the plot was exposed he was ordered to die and the fief was abolished.

literal: Son Ti succeeded and became Governor of Liangzhou.
idiomatic: His son Ti inherited the line and became Governor of Liangzhou.

literal: Because of greedy excess his title was cut off, punishment was added, and he was banished to the Northern Garrison.
idiomatic: For greed and license his title was stripped, further penalties imposed, and he was sent to the Northern Garrison.

literal: After long time Ti's son staff attendant Ying removed his cap and requested to resign his post to take his father's place on the frontier — Emperor Xiaowen did not permit it.
idiomatic: Long afterward Ti's son Ying, a staff attendant, begged to resign his office and take his father's frontier post; Emperor Xiaowen refused.

literal: Later on the southern campaign Ti accompanied the imperial carriage.
idiomatic: Later, on the southern campaign, Ti accompanied the emperor.

literal: At Luoyang he participated in settling the plan to move the capital.
idiomatic: At Luoyang he took part in deciding the capital transfer.

literal: Soon he died; because he had shared in the merit of moving the capital he was posthumously enfeoffed Marquis of Changxiang.
idiomatic: He soon died; for helping move the capital he was posthumously made Marquis of Changxiang.

literal: In the reign of Emperor Xuanwu he was posthumously given Governor of Yongzhou, posthumous title "Yi."
idiomatic: Under Emperor Xuanwu he was posthumously made Governor of Yongzhou with the posthumous name Yi.

literal: Son Yu, courtesy name Wenruo, succeeded to the fief.
idiomatic: His son Yu, courtesy name Wenruo, inherited the fief.

literal: Yu in youth had literary talent and at the time was greatly admired.
idiomatic: Yu was gifted in letters from youth and was widely admired.

literal: Attendant-in-ordinary Cui Guang saw him and said to others: "A dark-haired Three-Dukes — it will be this man."
idiomatic: Attendant-in-ordinary Cui Guang saw him and said, "Here is a young man who will reach the Three Excellencies."

literal: In youth together with his cousin Prince of Anfeng Yanming and Prince of Zhongshan Xi, all being of the imperial clan with broad learning in the classics and literature equally famous — at the time people could not settle their relative excellence.
idiomatic: In youth he and his cousins Prince of Anfeng Yanming and Prince of Zhongshan Xi, all imperial clansmen learned in the classics, were equally famed; contemporaries could not rank them.

literal: Secretariat Gentleman Fan Yang Lu Daojiang said to Personnel Minister Qinghe Cui Xiu: "The three men's learning and talent are all excellent and beautiful, yet Anfeng is lacking in quick repartee, Zhongshan has too much black-and-white distinction, not equal to Jinan's flowing grace and easy elegance."
idiomatic: Secretariat Gentleman Lu Daojiang of Fanyang told Personnel Minister Cui Xiu of Qinghe: "All three are brilliant, but Anfeng lacks quick wit, Zhongshan argues too much in black and white — neither matches Jinan's easy grace."

literal: At the time people made a saying of it: "The three kings are Chu jade, yet not equal to Jinan's full squareness."
idiomatic: People said: "The three princes are Chu jade, but none equals Jinan's completeness."

literal: Yu's bearing was leisurely and ample, his utterance flowing and beautiful.
idiomatic: Yu's manner was relaxed and ample; his speech flowed beautifully.

literal: Prince of Langye Wang Song, a man with a famous name, whenever he saw him never failed to be heart-intoxicated and forget weariness.
idiomatic: Prince of Langye Wang Song, a man of renown, never met him without losing himself in delight and forgetting fatigue.

literal: He submitted hymns for the Zheng temple — at the time called beautiful.
idiomatic: He submitted temple hymns for the Zheng shrine; they were praised at court.

literal: Appointed Palace Attendant Yellow Gate Attendant.
idiomatic: He was appointed Supervising Attendant of the Yellow Gate.

literal: Yu's original given name was Liang, courtesy name Shimming; at the time Attendant-in-ordinary Mu Shao shared office with Yu and to avoid Shao's father's taboo name submitted requesting a name change.
idiomatic: Yu's original name was Liang, courtesy Shimming; Attendant-in-ordinary Mu Shao shared his office and, to avoid Shao's father's taboo, asked that Yu be renamed.

literal: Edict said: "Shimming's spirit and bearing transport and flow, often comparing himself to Xun Wenruo — may be named Yu, to take the fixed form of equal standing in stature."
idiomatic: The edict said: "Shimming's bearing is lofty and fluent; he compares himself to Xun Yu — let him be named Yu, to match that stature."

literal: Yu requested restoration of his original fief; edict permitted restoration of Linhuai, provisioned from Xiangzhou Weijun.
idiomatic: Yu asked to recover his original fief; the court restored Linhuai, with provisions from Weijun in Xiangzhou.

literal: He also long served concurrently as Censor Commandant.
idiomatic: He long served concurrently as Censor Commandant.

literal: Yu considered the order of seniority correctly obtained and did not decline.
idiomatic: Yu thought the appointment proper by seniority and did not decline.

literal: Army Supervisor Yu Zhong was resentful and spoke to the court: "Though Linhuai again has flowing grace to be viewed, he lacks the backbone of firm integrity — the Censor's post, I fear he is not fit for it."
idiomatic: Army Supervisor Yu Zhong, resentful, told the court: "Linhuai may look elegant, but he lacks backbone — I doubt he can bear the censor's office."

literal: He thereupon removed his insignia, returning in a single cart — the court currents sighed for him.
idiomatic: Yu thereupon set aside his insignia and returned in a plain cart; court opinion sighed over him.

literal: Promoted in stages to Attendant-in-ordinary, Guard General, Left Honored Grandee, concurrently Left Vice Director of the Secretariat, overseeing selection.
idiomatic: He rose through Attendant-in-ordinary, Guard General, and Left Honored Grandee to concurrent Left Vice Director of the Secretariat, overseeing appointments.

literal: Later with his original office he became Eastern Route Commissioner.
idiomatic: Later he became Eastern Route Commissioner while keeping his prior offices.

literal: When Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang and killed the Yuan clan, Yu beat his breast and wept bitterly, then fled to Liang.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang and slaughtered the Yuan, Yu beat his breast and wept, then fled to Liang.

literal: Emperor Wu of Liang sent his attendant Chen Jiansun to receive him and also observe Yu's person.
idiomatic: Emperor Wu of Liang sent his attendant Chen Jiansun to welcome him and take his measure.

literal: Jiansun called Yu's spirit bearing leisurely and handsome.
idiomatic: Jiansun reported that Yu's bearing was easy and handsome.

literal: Wu of Liang had also earlier heard his name and deeply prized and awaited him.
idiomatic: The Liang emperor had already heard of him and valued him highly.

literal: Seeing Yu at Leyou Garden, thereupon a banquet with music was set.
idiomatic: He received Yu at Leyou Garden and gave a banquet with music.

literal: Yu hearing the music sighed and wept, tears crossing — Wu of Liang for it was not pleased.
idiomatic: Yu sighed and wept at the music; the emperor was displeased.

literal: Of those before and after who fled and rebelled, all waited on instruction to call Wei false — only Yu in memorials always said Prince of Linhuai of Wei.
idiomatic: Other defectors called Wei a false dynasty at court's cue; only Yu in his memorials still wrote Prince of Linhuai of Wei.

literal: Wu of Liang honored Yu's refined nature and did not blame him for it.
idiomatic: The Liang emperor respected Yu's refinement and did not reproach him.

literal: When he learned Emperor Zhuangang had ascended the throne, Yu because his mother was old requested return — his words earnest and cutting.
idiomatic: Learning that Emperor Zhuangang had taken the throne, Yu begged to return because his mother was old; his plea was urgent and sharp.

literal: Wu of Liang prized his talent yet found it hard to go against his intention and sent his Vice Director Xu Mian privately to urge Yu to stay.
idiomatic: The emperor prized his talent but could not refuse his wish; he sent Vice Director Xu Mian privately to persuade him to stay.

literal: Yu said: "In death I would still wish the north — how much more in life?"
idiomatic: Yu said, "Even in death I would choose the north — how much more while I live?"

literal: Wu of Liang thereupon sent him off with ceremony.
idiomatic: The Liang emperor then sent him home with full ceremony.

literal: Yu's nature was utmost filial.
idiomatic: Yu was deeply filial.

literal: From the time of separation he took no wine or meat;
idiomatic: From the day he left his mother he took no wine or meat;

literal: His haggard countenance — those who saw him were wounded by it.
idiomatic: his face grew haggard; all who saw him were moved.

literal: He held posts Minister Director of Affairs, Grand Marshal, concurrently Recorder of the Secretariat.
idiomatic: He served as Minister Director, Grand Marshal, and concurrent Recorder of the Secretariat.

literal: Emperor Zhuangang posthumously honored Martial Emperor Wu of Xuan as Cultured and Solemn Emperor, temple name Su Ancestor, mother Consort Li as Cultured and Solemn Empress.
idiomatic: Emperor Zhuangang posthumously honored Martial Emperor Wu of Xuan as Cultured and Solemn Emperor, temple name Su Ancestor, and his mother Consort Li as Cultured and Solemn Empress.

literal: When about to move the imperial tablets to the Ancestral Temple, making Emperor Xiaowen a father's younger brother in worship.
idiomatic: When the court prepared to move their spirit tablets into the Ancestral Temple, it treated Emperor Xiaowen as a father's younger brother in the rites.

literal: Yu memorialized remonstrance, considering that: "Han founder created the enterprise — Xiang Street had the Grand Supreme's temple;
idiomatic: Yu remonstrated in a memorial: "When the Han founder began the enterprise, Xiang Street held the Grand Supreme's temple;

literal: Guangwu in the restoration — Nandun had established Chunling's shrine.
idiomatic: when Guangwu restored the house, Nandun had Chunling's shrine.

literal: Emperor Yuan to Emperor Guangwu was distant, severed mourning — yet still personally upheld the son's way, entering to succeed the great lineage.
idiomatic: Emperor Yuan to Guangwu was only a distant kinsman, past the mourning limit, yet still served him as a son and entered the great lineage.

literal: Emperor Gaozu to the sacred person was in kinship really like son — Your Majesty having already inherited the great succession, how can you add the father's younger brother's name?
idiomatic: Gaozu to Your Majesty's person was in truth like father to son; having inherited the great succession, how can you add a father's younger brother to the temple?

literal: Moreover when Han Xuandi succeeded Emperor Xiaozhao, that was making a younger uncle the superior ancestor — how could he forget the lineage's receiving the father and mother in worship?
idiomatic: When Han Xuandi succeeded Xiaozhao, he elevated a younger uncle — yet he did not forget the lineage that received father and mother in sacrifice.

literal: It was because the great principle was thus displaced.
idiomatic: Great principle overrode kinship.

literal: When Jin's Virtue was about to rise, Prince Xuan received commission, Prince Jing's intent lay in destroying the crown, Prince Wen's heart schemed splitting the cap.
idiomatic: When Jin's mandate rose, Prince Xuan took the regency; Prince Jing aimed to cast off the crown; Prince Wen plotted to split the realm.

literal: Though in sacrifice it was still Wei as ruler, power returned to Jin's house.
idiomatic: Sacrifice still named Wei, but power passed to Jin.

literal: Kun and Ji in fact overturned Cao's clan.
idiomatic: Sima Kun and Ji in fact overturned the Cao house.

literal: Moreover Ziyuan was Prince Xuan's tomb progeny, Prince Wen completed his great enterprise.
idiomatic: Ziyuan was Xuan's line from the tomb; Wen finished the great enterprise.

literal: Therefore Jin Wudi succeeded literary ancestor and martial ancestor — Xuan rightly had the father's younger brother's designation.
idiomatic: Thus Jin Wudi succeeded the literary and martial ancestors; Xuan rightly bore the title of father's younger brother.

literal: Taking today as type of antiquity, I fear it may not be paired.
idiomatic: To compare today with that past, I fear the cases do not match.

literal: Emperor Gaozu — virtue overflowed within the seas, the Way surpassed beyond all.
idiomatic: Emperor Gaozu's virtue filled the realm; his Way surpassed all bounds.
